ADVERTISEMENT. 


In  Books  which  are  published  as  Guides  to  Travellers,  Accuracy 
must  ever  be  regarded  as  the  principal  object ;  the  Proprietor 
therefore  thinks  it  incumbent  upon  him  to  state  the  Authorities 
under  which  this  Itinerary  was  first  published.  It  might,  per- 
haps, be  sufficient  to  say,  that  it  was  brought  forward  under  the 
sanction  of  His  Majesty's  Postmaster  General:  but  he  cannot 
avail  himself  of  such  an  indulgence  without  noticing  the  circum- 
stances which  procured  him  that  very  honourable  patronage. 

Having  had  it  in  command  from  the  Postmaster  General  to 
make  a  Survey,  under  the  direction  of  Mr.  Hasker,  Surveyor  and 
Superintendant  of  the  Mail  Coaches,  of  all  the  principal  Roads 
throughout  the  kingdom,  for  official  purposes,  the  accuracy  of 
which  fas  required  ly  an  Act  of  Queen  Anna,  for  all  Roads  mea- 
sured on  account  of  the  General  Post  Office)  is  attested  on  the 
oaths  of  the  several  Surveyors  employed,  it  was  deemed  to  be  a 
Work  of  such  utility  to  the  Public,  that  it  ought  not  to  be  with- 
held -,  as,  from  the  precision  with  which  it  was  executed,  much 
benefit  might  accrue  to  the  Traveller  j  and  as  the  distances  oh 
those  Roads  were  planned  from  one  stationary  object  to  another, 
it  would  enable  him  to  determine,  beyond  dispute,  the  exact 
length  of  his  stages. 

Extensive  as  was  this  Survey,  it  was  nevertheless  considered 
not  to  embrace  the  whole  of  those  Roads  to  which  the  Traveller 
might  wish  occasionally  to  refer  5  therefore  the  Proprietor  has,  with 
great  industry  and  care,  selected  from  the  County  Surveys  such 
ether  Roads  as  appeared  to  him  essential,  the  distances  on  which, 
although  not  regulated  by  his  own  Survey,  and,  of  course,  not 
calculated  from  one  stationary  mark  to  another,  yet  he  has  every 
reason  to  believe  are  faithful,  the  whole  being  verified  by  the  dif- 
ferent Postmasters  throughout  the  kingdom,  and  officially  com- 
municated by  letter  to  Francis  Freeling,  Esq.  Secretary  to 
the  General  Post  Office,  and  Thomas  Hasker,  Esq.  Superin- 
tendant of  the  Mail  Coaches,  and  by  them  forwarded  to  the 
Author.  Through  the  same  channel  he  also  received  a  List  of 
such  Inns  as  supply  Post  Horses  and  Carriages  (whioia  are  added 
at  the  end  of  each  Route),  Seats,  kc.  &c, 

+  FIFTH 


ADVERTISEMENT, 

FIFTH   EDITION. 

Anxious  to  preserve  the  good  opinion  of  the  Public,  the  Pro- 
prietor has  used  his  utmost  endeavours  to  correct  those  errors  to 
which  a  publication  of  this  description  must  always  be  liable  j  and 
he  has  so  arranged  the  Remarks  which  accompany  the  Roads,  as  that 
they  and  the  Route  to  which  they  refer,  present  themselves  to  the 
eye  of  the  reader  at  the  same  time. 

To  the  Population,  and  Number  of  Houses  in  each  Town, 
given  from  the  returns  made  to  Parliament — the  Time  of  the  Mail's 
Arrival  at  and  Departure  from  each  Town — the  specification  of 
the  corporate  Towns,  and  of  those  at  which  the  Assizes  are  held 
— the  Course  of  the  Rivers  crossed  on  the  Routes,  and  the  Line 
of  the  navigable  Canals,  describing  their  length,  and  showing  the 
places  through  which  they  pass — the  Inns  on  the  road  which  sup- 
ply Post  Horses  and  Carriages  -,  also,  those  Inns  in  the  Metropolis 
whence  the  Mail  a?id  Stage  Coaches  depart  (showing  the  Route  they 
take  by  reference  to  the  Itinerary  ;  the  Time  of  their  Departure 
from  London,  and  Arrival  at  their  respective  Inns  in  the  Country  ; 
likewise  the  Time  of  their  Departure  thence,  and  Arrival  in  Town) 
— several  additional  Cross  Roads — the  Circuits  of  the  Judges— the 
Rates  of  Postage  in  Great  Britain — a  List  of  the  Stages  going  from 
London  to  the  circumjacent  Villages,  &c. — with  Maps  of  the  Isle 
of  Wight,  the  Environs  of  London,  Bath,  Brighton,  Margate, 
and  Cheltenham,  is  made  the  following 

IMPORTANT    ADDITION: 

Routes  to  upwards  of  Nine  Thousand  Places,  lying  off  from  the 
main  Roads,  and  which  will  not  be  found  in  any  other  work  of 
this  description. 


SIXTH    EDITION. 

The  approbation  of  the  Public,  testified  by  the  rapid  sale  of  the 
preceding  *  Editions,  is  a  source  of  pleasing  satisfaction  to  the 
Author.  He  once  more  tenders  his  grateful  acknowledgments 
for  the  verv  flattering  patronage  which  he  has  received. 

A  new  impression  of  the  Itinerary  being  called  for,  it  is 
deemed  necessary  to  state  that  the  whole  work  has  been  revised 
with  care  and  diligence  ;  a  few  new  Roads,  Direct  as  well  as 
Cross,  have  been  added  ;  great  pains  have  been  taken  to  render 
the  account  of  the  Gentlemen's  Seats  correct  to  the  present 
period  ;  the  Population  of  the  Towns,  &c.  is  given  according  to 
the  last  returns  made  to  Parliament  (m  1811)  j  and  wherever  an 
improvement,  either  important  or  minute,  has  presented  itself, 
or  been  suggested  by  friends,  it  has  beeR  adopted.

DIRECT   ROADS 

That  the  Distances  may  correspond  as  nearly  as  possible  with 
the  Milestones  on  these  Roads,  they  are  reckoned  from  th"  cus- 
tomary Standards. 

At  the  conclusion  of  each  Route,  where  the  length  is  such  as 
to  render  it  useful,  a  Return  Route  is  added,  exhibiting  at  one 
view  the  immediate  distance  from  stage  to  stage,  without  the 
trouble  of  subtracting;  to  which  method  of  calculation  the  Tra- 
veller would  otherwise  find  it  necessary  to  resort.  The  reckoning 
on  this  Back  Route  is  also  continued  to  the  General  Post  Office, 
for  the  purpose  of  preserving  the  plan  of  the  First  Edition  to  those 
who  may  consider  it  essential.

CROSS   ROADS. 

To  this  part  of  the  Work  great  Additions  have  also  been  made, 
and  numerous  Roads  introduced,  which  are  not  described  in  any 
other  publication  of  this  nature.— The  Index  to  these  Roads  is 
likewise  so  arranged  as  to  afford  an  easy  and  direct  reference  to 
€ach  Route. 


SEATS. 

The  Proprietor  has  to  acknowledge  infinite  obligations  to  his 
Friends  for  numerous  Additions  and  Corrections,  which  they  have 
kindly  communicated,  and  which  have  enabled  him  to  extend  his 
List  of  Seats,  and  render  it  as  perfect  as  the  nature  of  the  Work 
will  admit  j  but  as  this  part  of  the  Publication  is  necessarily  liable 

a  to 


ADVERTISEMENT. 

to  some  inaccuracies,  even  during  its  printing,  he  hopes  thai, 
where  any  errors  may  be  perceived,  they  will  not  be  imputed  to. 
negligence,  as  the  utmost  care  has  been  taken  to  render  the  List 
correct ;  and  he  earnestly  entreats  those  who  may  do  him  the  honour 
of  making  this  Book  their  travelling  Companion,  that  they  wilt 
have  the  goodness  to  transmit  any  additional  information  for  the- 
improvement  of  the  work  ;  and  their  communications  shall  be 
carefully  attended  to  and  gratefully  acknowledged.  A  full  and 
complete  Index  to  the  Seats  is  given  at  the  end  of  the  Work,, 
with  particular  reference  to  the  page  where  they  are  noticed. 


MAP. 

The  Map  of  England  and  Wales,  which  accompanies,  has  been 
executed  with  the  utmost  oare  and  attention,  and  exhibits  the 
whole  of  the  Roads  contained  in  this  Work,  particularly  describing 
those  on  which  the  Mail  Coaches  travel. 

Figures  of  Reference  are  added  to  the  Cross  Roads,  correspond- 
ing with  the  number  of  the  Route  wherein  they  are  described  j 
thus  affording  an  additional  Index  to  those  Roads,  and  giving 
facility  to  the  Traveller  in  tracing  his  Route  in  every  direction, 
and  to  any  extent. 

Surveyors  employed  in  measuring  the  Roads  described  in  this  Work. 

George  Gretton,  Liverpool. 
Richard  Wollams,  Shirleywick. 
John  Burton,  Lancaster. 
Joseph  Singer,  Littletown,  Devon, 
L.  Hebert,  Strand. 

The  Measurements,  which  are  taken  in  miles  and  furlongs,  are 
arranged  in  columns  ;  the  first  and  second  giving  the  distance  from 
one  City,  Town,  or  Village,  to  the  next ;  the  third  and  fourth, 
the  number  of  miles  from  the  commencement  of  the  Road.

General  Directions  for  tracing  the  Roads, 

Suppose  you  want  the  Road  from  London  to  Doncaster — look 
for  the  name  of  that  place  in  the  Index  to  the  Direct  Roads  from 
London,  and  the  figure  opposite  to  it  (351)  refers  to  the  page  in 
"which  is  that  part  of  the  Road  containing  Doncaster,  though  the 
description  of  the  Road  in  which  it  is  situated  (being  that  from 
London  to  Carlisle  and  Glasgow)  begins  in  page  343,  and  ends  in 
page  360. 

In  describing  the  lesser  Roads  branching  from  the  greater,  the 
last  remarkable  place  on  the  great  Road,  or  the  spot  where  the 
lesser  turns  off,  is  first  given,  with  a  reference  to  the  page  in  which 
you  will  find  the  Road  so  far  as  to  that  place  j  and  afterwards  the 
Branch  is  continued  :  as,  for  instance,  to  find  the  Road  from 
London  to  Weymouth,  the  Index  refers  you  for  Weymouth  to 
page  84,  where  you  find  it  in  the  following  form,  viz. 

M    F       M    F 

To  Dorchester,  p.  56 119  6 

Brodeway  4  7  124  5 

Melcomb  Regis  25  127  2 

Weymouth  —  4  127  6 

By  which  it  appears  you  are  referred  to  page  56  for  this  Road  as 
far  as  Dorchester  (the  last  remarkable  place  on  the  great  Road)  j 
and  the  remainder  of  the  Road  to  Weymouth  is  given  after  the 
above  form  in  page  84*  as  directed  by  the  Index.  These  Refer- 
ences are  made  use  of  in  order  to  prevent  the  numberless  repeti- 
tions, which  would  otherwise  unavoidably  occur,  and  thereby  swell 
the  Book  to  an  inconvenient  size. 

The  Index  to  the  Cross  Roads,  it  is  conceived,  is  so  copious  an<i 
explicit,  as  to  require  no  further  explanation  than  what  is.  given  at 
the  beginning  of  it.

Having 


Having  he/ore  observed  how  much  he  should  feel  olliged  to  those 
Travellers  who  would  do  him  the  favour  to  communicate  notice  of 
any  Error  which  they  may  occasionally  detect  in  this  Work,  it  may 
appear  intrusive  again  to  soticit  their  attention  ;  hut  the  Proprietor 
hopes  his  anxiety  will  he  excused,  in  consideration  of  the  advantage 
which  the  Puhlic  must  feel,  in  having  a  Work  of  this  nature  correct 
in  all  its  parts,  and  that  to  render  it  so  exceeds  the  possibility  of  in- 
dividual exertion — In  the  performance  of  this  task,  he  has  used  his 
utmost  endeavours  to  make  his  Book  complete,  and  flatters  himself, 
that  in  the  Delineation  of  the  Roads  few  errors  will  he  found  ;  but 
it  scarcely  needs  remark,  that  in  giving  the  numerous  Seats  which 
this  Work  describes,  some  mistakes  must  occur,  to  rectify  which,  he 
takes  the  liberty  of  observing,  that  nothing  can  so  effectually  con- 
tribute, as  the  information  of  the  intelligent  Traveller,  whose 
assistance  he  most  particularly  requests  ;  as  also  that  of  Gentlemen 
of  local  information,  to  whom  he  would  consider  himself  highly 
indebted  for  their  communications 9  to  which  the  utmost  attention 
will  be  paid. 

It  would  add  to  the  obligation,  if  Gentlemen,  when  they  com- 
municate information,  would  have  the  goodness  to  sign  their 
Name  and  Address,  as  it  frequently  happens  that  further  expla- 
nation is  necessary,  and  it  would  remove  any  doubt  as  to  authen- 
ticity.

TABLES,  shewing  the  immediate  Route  from  the  Metropolis  to 

upwards  of  9,000  Places  lying  off  from  the  Main  Roads 

throughout  England  and  Wales. 

The  following:  Tables  are  intended  to  shew  the  immediate  Route  from  the  Metro- 
polis to  those  places  which,  lying  off  from  the  Main  Road,  could  not  be  described 
in  the  body  of  the  work.  References  are  added  shewing  the  Route  to  be  taken  by 
the  Traveller,  as  also  the  place  on  the  road  nearest  to  that  which  is  sought. 

EXAMPLE  :— Suppose  you  want  the  Road  from  London  to  Abberdiall, — refer  for 
that  place  in  this  Table,  and  you  will  find  it  described  2  mis.  /  (2  miles  to  the  left) 
of  Longhope,  which  place,  as  arranged  in  the  next  column,  will  be  found  in  page 
196,  and  your  Route  will  therefore  be  directed  through  Uxbridge,  Beaconslield, 
High  Wycombe,  Oxford,  Witney,  Northleach,  Cheltenham,  and  Gloucester,  to 
Longhope,  where,  as  expressed  in  the  Table,  you  turn  to  the  left,  and  at  about  the 
distance  of  2  miles  is  situate  Abbenhall. 

Note.  In  selecting  the  roads  to  which  the  references  are  made,  we  have  con- 
sidered it  an  accommodation  to  select  those  (ivhen  it  could  be  done)  on  which  stage- 
coaches travel — it  may  also  be  proper  to  observe  that  where  the  traveller  may  re- 
quire to  be  forwarded  by  Post  chaise,  he  must  oftentimes  stop  short  of  our  refer- 
ence, or  otherwise  procee'd  to  the  next  stage  beyond  it — as  in  the  above  example,  he 
must  either  stop  at  Gloucester,  or  proceed  to  Ross,  the  next  stage  from  Gloucester. 

The  direction  r  and  I  are  not  to  be  understood  always  to  mean  directly  right  and 
left  of  the  places  referred  to,  but  right  and  left  of  the  road  on  which  you  are  travel 
ling,  as  the  places  sought  will  in  many  instances  lie  forward,  or  obliquely,  of  the 
reference,  in  a  direction  thus, 

in  such  case,  we  have  signified  the  same  by  adding  an  o  to 
=         the  letters  r  and  I. — Thus  r.  o.  ri'ght  oblique,  I.  o.  left  ob- 
lique.

INDEX    OF    PLACES 

WHICH    OCCUR    IN    THE    ROUTES  OF  THE  DIFFERENT 
'    COACHES    GOING    FROM    THE    METROPOLIS. 

Places  printed  in  the  Roman  Character  are  those  through  which  Coaches  pas> 
in  the  Prosecution  of  their  Journey  to  some  Town  more  remote  from  the 
Metropolis. 

The  italic  Character  denotes  that  there  are  Coaches  whose  Journeys  terminate 
at  the  Place ;  the  References  to  such  Coaches  are  printed  within  Brackets 
[]:  where  other  Figures  follow  those  included  within  the  Brackets,  they 
relate  to  Coaches  which  pass  through  the  Place. 

m.  following  the  Figure  of  Reference,  signifies  the  Mail  Coach. 

The  Numbers  opposite  the  Name  of  each  Place  correspond  with  those 
annexed  to  the  Coaches  in  the  List  of  Inns  which  immediately  succeeds 
this  Index. 

EXAMPLE. 

Supposing  a  Conveyance  to  Abberford  to  be  wanted — see  in  this  Index  the 
Name  of  Abberford,  and  the  Numbers  opposite,  176.  395,  520; — turn  to 
either  of  these  Numbers  in  the  List  of  Inns,  where  will  be  found  the  Coach 
which  passes  through  that  Place ;  viz.  [176],  Aberdeen  and  Edinburgh  Coach, 
Bull  and  Mouth  Inn  ;  &c.  &c.

A  LIST 

OF    ALL    THE 

INJSIS  THROUGHOUT  THE  METROPOLIS 

FROM    WHICH    THE 

MAIL  AND  OTHER  STAGE  COACHES  DEPART: 

Showing  the  Route  they  take  by  Reference  to  the  Itinerary  5 
the  Time  of  their  Departure  from  London,  and  Arrival  at  their 
respective  Inns  in  the  Country  5  likewise  the  Time  of  their 
Departure  thence,  and  Arrival  in  Town. 


*^*  The  following  List  has  been  examined  by  the  respective  Proprietors,  and  by 
them  reported  correct. — The  Publisher,  nevertheless,  thinks  it  proper  to  observe., 
that  notwithstanding  the  care  which  he  has  taken  to  avoid  every  species  of  error, 
it  ivill  sometimes  happen,  from  a  change  of  Route,  &c.  that  an  inaccuracy  may 
occur  ;  he  therefore  suggests  the  propriety  of  such  inquiry  at  the  Inn  as  may  he 
f hough  t  necessary,  in  order  to  secure  the  Traveller  from  mistake.

ABBREVIATIONS,    &C.    USED    IN    THIS    WORK, 

T.  G.  Turnpike  Gate.

R.  River. 

Cities  and  Market  Towns  are  printed  in  Capital  Letters: — Cities  are  besides 
distinguished  by  a  c  prefixed,  Borough  Towns  by  a  b,  and  Towns  and  Places 
where  Post  Offices  or  Receiving  Houses  are  established,  by  a  p. 

H.  and  I.  for  Houses  and  Inhabitants :  the  Figures  added  thereto  express  the  Number 
of  each  'which  the  Place  contains,  agreeably  to  the  Population  Act  of  1811. 

The  x  affixed  to  the  Names  of  Places  denotes  that  in  or  near  them  there  is 
some  remarkable  Object,  which  is  noticed  in  the  Observations  accompany- 
ing the  Route. 

The  Word  in  Italic  immediately  following  the  Place  to  which  the  Measurement 
is  directed,  implies  the  Point  opposite  to  which  it  is  given. 

Roads  described  as  diverging  from  the  main  Route  are  to  be  considered  as 
Turnpike  Roads  leading  to  the  Places  to  which  they  are  directed,  unless 
otherwise  expressed. 

N.  B.  The  Inns  at  the  different  Places  on  each  Road  -which  supply  Post  Horses  and 
Carriages  are  selected,  and  given  at  the  End  of  every  Route;  but  the  Arrange- 
ment of  them  is  not  intended  to  convey  any  Preference. 

On  the  Map  -which  accompanies  this  Work,  are  also  distinguished  those  Roads  on 
'which  the  Mail  Coaches  travel :  and  to  the  Cross  Roadi  Figures  are  added t  de- 
noting the  Route  'wherein  they  occur.

Front  is  a  Polygon ;  its  Angles  five

tagons of  60  Feet  at  the  Ends,  and  t  he 
Entrance  200  Feet.  The  Pier  forms 
the  grand  Promenade.  Ramsgate  is 
much  frequented  as  a  Bathing-place.

Salisbury,  a  City  and  Bishop's  See,  was 
first  incorporated  by  Henry  III.;  is

sidered the  most  elegant  and  regular 
Gothic  Structure  in  the  Kingdom, 
and  its  Spire  the  tallest,  being  410 
Feet  high ;  on  the  large  east  Window 
is  a  Painting  of  the  Resurrection,  by 
Mr.  Pearson,  from  a  Design  of  Sir 
Joshua  Reynolds  ;  on  the  small  east 
Window,  a  Painting  of  the  Elevation 
of  the  Brazen  Serpent,  the  Gift  of 
the  Earl  of  Radnor.  The  Market 
Place  is  very  extensive,  and  in  the 


1  south  east  Corner  stands  the  new 
Council  House,  a  magnificent  Struc- 
ture, erected  at  the  Expense  of  the 
Earl  of  Radnor,  and  completed 
1 795  ;  in  it  the  Assizes  and  the  Ses 
sions  of  the  Peace  are  held  for  the 
City  and  County.

Southampton,  a  Place  of  great  fashionable 
Summer  Resort,  was  incorporated  by 
Charles  I.  under  a  Mayor,  Aldermen, 
Recorder,  Sheriff',  Common  Council, 
&c.  The  Mayor  is  Admiral  of  the 
Liberties.  This  Borough  was  made 
by  Henry  II.  and  by  King  John 
County  of  itself:  it  returns  2  Mem- 
bers to  Parliament,  elected  by  the 
Inhabitants  at  large,  paying  Scot 
and  Lot :  the  Number  of  Voters 
about  6 co.  Near  the  west  Quay  is 
a  Range  of  commodious  Baths,  in 
which  the  Water  is  changed  every 
Tide :  here  is  also  a  convenient 
warm  Bath.  The  publ:c  Rooms  are 
situate  near  the  Baths,  where  are 
held  the  Summer  Assemblies;  those 
in  the  Winter  are  held  at  the  Dol- 
phin Inn.

A  Mail  Packet  goes  from  Southampton  to  Coives,  Isle  of  Wight,  every  Morning  at 
7  o'  Clock,  and  returns  from  Coives  to  Southampton  every  Afternoon  at  3  ;  and  another 
Packet  sails  at  9,  which  returns  at  £  past  3.  Distance  5  Leagues. — A  Packetalso  sails 
from  Portsmouth  for  Ryde  immediately  on  the  Arrival  of  the  Mail  from  London  at  the 
former  Place  ;  and  another  sails  on  the  Arrival  of  the  Bye  and  Cross  Road  Correspond- 
ence at  Portsmouth  :  the  first  is  about  8  in  the  Morning  ;  the  last  depends  upon  tht 
Arrival  of  Cross  Road  Letters.   Returns  from  Ryde  to  Portsmouth  about  §  past  J^  or  5

cuitous Route?,  calculated  to  exhibit  its  Beauties  :  and  for  those  who  may  be 
desirous  of  a  more  direct  Course,  another  Road  is  sriven  to  the  same  Place,

The  following  circuitous  Route  (with  Remarks)  is  communicated  to  us  by  a  Resident, 
as  a  most  delightful  Ride  for  those  who  wish  to  see  the  Beauties  of  the  Isle  of  Wight. 

From  Ryde  to  St.  John's  1  m.  ;  by  Westbrook  to  the  Priory  3  u. ;  to  St. 
Helen's  1  M. ;  over   St.  Helen's  Green,  and  North  Marsh,  to  Brading  4  M.j

Roads  measured  from  Hyde  Park  Corner. 


[92 

lover  Garbridge,  Sandown  Level,  and  Royal  Heath,  to  Shankiin,  4  m.;  and  by 
jLuccomb  to  Bonchurch  2  M.;  to  Steephill  1  m.;  St.  Lawrence  1  m.  3  by  the 
Chuich,  the  left  Hand  Road  immediately  under  the  Cliffs,  to  Mirables,  \\  u 
and  to  Niton,  i4  ;  to  Knowles  and  Pitlands.  Turn  at  the  Direction  to  the  left 
instead  of  the  right  Hand  (which  takes  you  to  Niton),  over  St.  Catherine's 
I  Down  toChale,  2  m.;  cross  Chale  Green  to  Shorewell,  4S  m.;  to  Brixton,  2  m.; 
i  Mottiston,  2  m.;  by  Brook  House  and  Church,  and  Shalcomb  Farm,  to 
JThorley,  3  m.;  to  Yarmouth  2  ti,  If  to  the  Needles,  take  the  first  Turnin 
on  the  left  beyond  Brook  Church  over  Compton  Down  and  Aston  Down,  to 
Freshwater  Gate  Inn,  and  at  the  Back  of  the  Inn  over  the  Cliffs  between  the 
Beacon  and  Warren  House  to  the  Lighthouse  at  the  Needier.. 

From  Shorewell  a  beautiful  Bridle  Road  goes  all  the  Way  over  Brixton, 
Shalcomb,  Tapne),  and  Aston  Downs,  in  a  direct  Line  to  Freshwater  Gate 
Inn,  the  Needles,  and  Yarmouth. 

The  following  Gentlemen's  Seats  and  romantic  Scenery  are  very  highly  de 
serving  the  Notice  of  the  picturesque  Traveller : 

By  Yaverland,  Hermit's  Hole,  a  curious  Cavity  in  the  Culvers  Cliff  imme 
diately  over  the  Sea.     By  Sandown  Level,  the  Fort. 

At  Shankiin,  the  Chine,  a  remarkably  beautiful  Chasm,  with  a  Fall  of  Water. 

By  Luccomb,  the  Chine,  next  the  Sea,  singularly  interesting  for  its  Wildness. 

At  St.  Lawrence,  the  highly-finished  Cottage  of  the  late  Sir  Richard  Worsley, 
ornamented  with  a  Vineyard,  now  the  Hon.  C.  A.  Pelham. 

Mirables  is  wonderfully  romantic,  and  singularly  interesting  for  its  very 
picturesque  Walks,  and  bold  uninterrupted  Views  of  the  Ocean,  on  which  is 
closely  situated  the  Cottage  of  G.  Arnold,  Esq. :  Knowles  and  Pitlands,  rude 
tremendous  rocky  Scenery,  with  fine  Water  breaking  immediately  from  under 
the  stupendous  Cliffs  of  St.  Catherine's,  rendered  singularly  awful  by  its  recent 
violent  Convulsions  of  the  whole  surrounding  Rocks  and  Soil  for  a  considerable 
Extent,  having  destroyed  a  Cottage,  and  overthrown  several  immense  Rocks. 

At  Aston,  Capt.  Urry's  ;  and  at  Yarmouth  another  Seat  of  Cap::.  Urry's. 

\  m.  beyond  Knowles  and  Pitlands  is  Black  Gang,  a  tremendous  Chasm.

The  Worcester  and  Birmingham  Canal 
commences  at  the  Severn,  close  to 
Worcester  ;  the  whole  Line  is  not 
yet  completed,  but  its  intended 
Course,  agreeably  to  the  Act  for  exe 
cuting  it,  is  near  to  Droitwich,  Stoke 
Prior,  Tardebig,  Alvechurch,  King's 
Norton,  and  thence  to  Birmingham 

Worcester  is  situated  upon  the  River  Se 
vern,  and  is  much  famed  for  its  fine 
Manufacture  of  China,  and  its  an- 
cient Cathedral,  which  is  410  Feet 
in  Length,  and  78  in  Breadth,  and 
the  Tower  196  Feet  high.  The 
Nave  is  extremely  beautiful,  both 
in  Style  and  Proportions.  There 
are  several  handsome  Monuments, 
but  the  chief  is  that  of  King  John, 
standing  in  the  Midst  of  the  Choir. 
His  Majesty,  in  1789,  attended  the 
Music  Meeting,  in  Commemoration 
of  which  was  rebuilt  the  Window  in 
the  west  Front.

Bristol  is  situated  on  the  Rivers  Avon; 
and  Frome ;  it  is  a  City  and  Countyj 
of  itself,  and  King  Henry  VIII. ; 
made  it  a  Bishopric.  The  Interior  of! 
the  City  is  close,  but  in  the  Suburbs 
and  external  Parts  are  elegant  and 
spacious  Buildings.  Carts  are  not 
admitted  in  the  Streets,  for  fear  of 
damaging  the  Arches  of  the  Vaults, 
&c.  made  under-ground  for  convey- 
ing the  Soil  int©  the  Rivers  ;  and  on 
this  Account  every  Thing  is  carried 
by  Sledges.  From  Redcliffe  Parade 
is  a  most  beautiful  View  of  the  sur- 
rounding Country.  It  has  a  very 
extensive  Quay,  and  a  Dock,  which 
will  contain  ten  Sail  of  large 
Vessels ;  and  another  of  an  inferior 
Size.  The  Cathedral  was  founded 
in  1 140.  The  Hot  Wells  are  1  m. 
below  the  City,  close  by  the  River  ; 
their  Waters  are  reckoned  specific 
for  the  Diabetes,  phthisical,  scorbu- 
tic, and  inflammatory  Disordeis.

Newport,  the  Monmouth  Canal,  where 
is  its  Basin,  which  connects  with 
the  Usk  R.  and  through  its  Channel 
unites  the  Navigation  with  the  Se- 
vern. It  has  two  Branches — the 
Pontypool,  to  which  Town  it  goes, 
and  near  to  it  is  joined  with  the 
Brecknock  Canal  (whose  Course  is 
by  Abergavenny  and  along  by  the 
Side  of  the  R.  Usk  to  the  Town  of 
Brecon)  and  the  Crumlin,  which 
passes  by  Risca  to  Crumlin  Bridge. 
Length  of  the  Pontypool  Branch  1 1 
m.  falls  447  Feet ;  Crumlin  Branch

Ewenney, on  r.  the  Remains  of  the  Priory. 

At  Margam  are  the  Ruins  of  a  Cbaptei 
House;  and  on  r.  Margam  Park,  — 
Talbot,  Esq. 

2  M.  from  Margam,  on  1.  is  Tyncaia 
House.   Rev.  Dr.  Hunt. 

Within  \  m.  of  Bag/and,  on  r.  Bagland 
Hall,  —  Jones,   Esq. 

At  Briton  Ferry,  on  1.  Lord  Vernon. 

i-^  M.  from  Briton  Ferry,  on  r.  is  Eagle 
B   sh  House,  — Evans,  Esq. 

On  an  Eminence  near  Neath  is  Gnoll 
Castle,  —  Johnson,  Esq. 

Neath,  the  Neath  Canal :  it  is  united 
with  the  Neath  R.  (S.  of  the  Town), 
which  connects  it  with  Swansea  Bay; 
its  Course  North  is  close  by  the  Neath 
R.  and  extends  to  Abemant.  There 
is  a  Branch  of  some  Length,  West  of 
the  Taff.  Neath  has  two  extensive 
Copper  Works,  and  some  Iron  Forges ; 
and  the  Coal  Pits  in  the  Neighbour- 
hood are  the  Means  of  a  consider- 
able Trade  to  Bristol  and  London, 
the  River  Neath  being  navigable  for 
coasting  Vessels.  About  \  M.  from 
the  Town,  on  the  western  Side  of  the 
River,  are  the  picturesque  Remains 
of  the  Abbey  founded  by  Richard  de 
Granville  and  his  Wife,  for  Cistertian 
Monks  :  in  this  Abbey  Edward  II 
took  Refuge  till  he  was  taken  by  the 
Earl  of  Leicester  in  1326.  It  is  a 
corporate  Town,  and  is  governed  by 
a  Portreeve,  12  Aldermen,  a  Re- 
corder, and  capital  Burgesses. 

1  m.  on  r.  of  Neath  is  Court  Herbert, 
—  Williams,  Esq.;  and  about  4  m. 
up  the  R.  Neath  is  Melincourt,  a 
famous  Waterfall. 

A  little  beyond  Llansamlet,  on  r.  Birch 
Grove,  late  —  Holbroke,  Esq. 

At  Morriston,  on  the  r.  is  Ciasemont, 
J.  Morris,  Esq. 

Swansea  :  the  Town,  built  on  a  semi- 
circular rising  Bank,  is  near  a  Mile 
and  a  Half  in  Length  ;  the  Houses 
are  modern  and  commodious,  and 
the  Streets  are  well  paved.  It  has  a 
Custom  House.  The  Remains  of  its 
ancient  Castle  are  converted  into  a 
Gaol  and  a  Workhouse.  Half  a 
Mile  from  the  Town,  on  the  Beach, 
stands  the  Bathing  House ;  there  are 
also  cold  and  hot  Sea-water  Baths 


near  the  Pottery  on  the  Strand.  The 
Trade  of  this  Town  is  considerably 
improved  by  means  of  the  Swansea 
Canal,  which,  uniting  with  the  R. 
Taff.  close  to  the  Town,  is  con- 
nected with  Swansea  Harbour,  and 
goes  from  thence  by  the  Side  of  the 
Taff  to  Hen  noyadd.  There  is  a 
Pottery  here  upon  Mr.  Wedgewood's 
Plan ;  an  Iron  Foundery ;  and  a 
good  dry  Dock.  It  has  a  consider- 
able Trade  in  the  Export  of  Stone, 
Coal,  Iron  Ore,  and  Limestone,  all 
found  on  the  Banks  of  the  Taff:  there 
are  also  seven  large  Copper  Houses 
some  Distance  from  the  Town,  smelt- 
ing annually  45,00©  Tons  of  Metal, 
and  consuming  70,000  Chaldrons  of 
Coal.  Swansea  is  governed  by  a  Port- 
reeve, 1 2  Aldermen,  2  Chamberlains, 
and  a  limited  Number  of  Burgesses. 

Forest  Bank,  on  r.  of,  is  Forest  Hall, 
Arthur  Davis,  Esq. 

Carmarthen  is  a  Place  of  great  Antiqui- 
ty, being  the  Maridunum  of  Ptolemy: 
it  was  once  fortified  with  Walls  and 
a  strong'  Castle,  Part  of  the  Gate 
now  only  remaining  $  and  the  County 
Gaol  occupies  its  Site,  handsomely 
built  of  hewn  Stone.  The  Church 
is  a  very  large  Building,  which,  with 
the  Churchyard,  is  surrounded  by  a 
Wall.  On  the  east  End  of  Priory 
Street  are  the  Ruins  of  a  Priory, 
founded  in  1148.  It  was  first  erect- 
ed into  a  Borough  by  Henry  VIII. 
and  sends  one  Member  to  Parlia- 
ment ;  and  James  I.  granted  it  a 
Charter  of.  Incorporation  as  a  Town 
and  County  of  itself,  with  Power  to 
make  Bye-laws :  it  is  governed  by  a 
Mayor,  6  Justices,  &e.  The  Prince 
of  Wales  has  here  his  Exchequer 
and  Chancery  for  South  Wales. 
There  are  several  Iron  and  Tin 
Mines  in  the  Neighbourhood,  and 
at  the  Entrance  of  Caermarthen  are 
Iron  and  Tin  Mills  belonging  to  John 
Morgan,  Esq.  ;  and  the  Smelting 
House  belonging  to  Lord  Cawdor. 

I  M.  from  Caermarthent  on  r.  is  Job's 
Well,  David  Edwardes,  Esq," 

Between  Tavernpl-atdeth  and  Pool  y 
Gravel,  on  r.  is  Wernallt  House,  — 
Williams,  Esq.

At  Charlton  Kings,W.  Hunt  Prinne, Esq. 

Near  Cheltenham,  at  Southam,  a  Seat 
of  the  ancient  Family  of  Delabere. 

Cheltenham  has  of  late  Years  greatly 
increased  in  its  Number  of  Buildings, 
and  is  become  a  Place  of  the  most 
fashionable  Resort,  on  account  of 
its  Waters  ;  they  are  impregnated 
with  Salts,  Sulphur,  Steel,  and  cal- 
careous Earth ;  and  operate  both  as 
a  Purgative  and  Restorative.  The 
Season  for  drinking  them  is  from 
May  to  October.  Its  Church  is  a 
venerable  Gothic  Structure,  and  the 
Churchyard  is  said  to  be  the  most 
commodious  in  England,  being  300 
Feet  in  Length,  with  double  Rows 
of  Lime-trees:  through  this  Walk 
you  pass  to  the  Spa: — the  Pump 
appears  under  a  Dome,  on  the  Left 
of  which  is  the  Breakfasting-room 
and  which  is  occasionally  converted 
into  a  Ball-room. 

~  M.west  of  Cheltenham,  on  an  Eminence, 
is  a  Seat  of  the  late  Earl  Fauconberg 
near  which  is  a  Spring,  discovered 
by  His  present  Majesty,  of  the  same 


Kind  of  Water  as  the  celebrated  Spa, 
but  of  a  stronger  Nature. 

Gloucester,  near,  Margaret  and  Maudlin 
Hospital,  founded  by  James  I. 

Gloucester ;  its  Cathedral  is  a  very  mag 
nincent  Specimen  of  Gothic  Archi 
tecturc  :  this  Fabric,  as  it  now  ap 
pears,  is  420  Feet  in  Length,  and  144 
in  Width  :  from  the  Centre  of  the 
Building  rises  a  majestic  Tower,  1 98 
Feet  in  Height,  surmounted  by  two 
beautifully  pierced  Pinnacles,  of  24 
Feet  in  Height.  The  Interior  of  the 
Cathedral  bears  a  solemn  and  im- 
pressive Aspect ;  the  Choir  is  very 
lofty,  and  in  a  narrow  Passage  over 
it  is  a  remarkable  Echo,  somewhat 
resembling  that  of  the  Whispering 
Gallery  of  St.  Paul's,  London.  The 
City  has  three  large  Suburbs,  and 
its  Boundaries  are  nearly  3  Miles  in 
Extent.  Besides  its  Cathedral  it  has 
five  Parish  Churches,  two  Grammar 
Schools,  two  commodious  Market 
Houses,  an  elegant  Theatre,  a  Cus- 
tom House,  and  a  County  Gaol  built 
after  the  Plan  of  Mr.  Howard. 

On  1.  of  Gloucester,  at  Matson,  William 
Fendol],  Esq.

Ledbury  to  the  City  of  Hereford.

Stratfor.i  on  Avon  : — This  Town  is  par- 
ticularly celebrated  as  the  Birthplace 
of  Shakspeare,  who  died  in  1616 
and  has  a  neat  Monument  in  the 
Church.  The  noted  Mulberry-tree 
which  grew  in  the  Gardens  of  the 
Author  was  destroyed  by  a  Successor, 
and  sold  to  a  Carpenter,  who  inge 
niously  worked  it  into  various  Orna- 
ments and  Trinkets.  Here  in  Sep 
tember  1769  was  the  first  Comme 
moration  of  Shakspeare's  Jubilee, 
when  an  Amphitheatre  was  erected 
on  the  Plan  of  Ranelagh,  for  the 
Reception  of  its  Visitors.  It  lasted 
three  Days,  during  which  Time  every 
Species  of  Entertainment  was  exhi- 
bited ;  such  as  Concerts,  Oratorios, 
Pageants,  Fireworks,  Illuminations, 
&c.  In  the  Guildhall  is  a  large  Room, 
called  Shakspeare's  Hall,  in  which 
are  two  excellent  Paintings  of  Shak- 
speare and  Garrick.  The  Church  is 
a  noble  Building,  with  a  lofty  Spire. 

The  Stratford  on  Avon  Canal  commences 
at  the  Town  of  Stratford  ;  has  a 
Branch  about  4  m.  from  it,  which 
goes  to  Benton,  passes  near  Henley 
in  Arden,  to  Lapworth,  where  a  Cut 
unites  it  with  the  Birmingham  Na- 
vigations ;  thence  to  Hockley  (where 
a  Branch  goes  to  Tamworth)  and 
King's  Norton,  where  it  unites  with 
the  Worcester  and  BirminghamCanal. 
\  M.  beyond  Stratford  on  Avon  is  Clop- 
ton  House,  John  Corbett,  Esq.

has  an  elegant  new  Theatre.  &c.

by  Robert  Montgomery  soon  after

round  Towers  now  remains.

nished), according  to  the  Plan  of  its 
Line,  commences  at  Shrewsbury, 
and  proceeds  close  to  Ellesmere,

it  goes  to  the  Mersey  River.  About

westry to  Ellesmere,  and  goes  near

Ludlow,  entering,  on  1.  Ludford  Park,: 
N.  L.  Charlton,  Esq. 

Ludlow  is  a  very  ancient  Town,  sends! 
two  Members  to  Parliament,  and  is] 
governed  by  2  Bailiffs  (who  are  thej 
returning  Officers),  12  Aldermen,! 
2nd  24  Common  Councilmen.  The 
Church  is  a  fine  venerable  Structure, 
built  of  Stone ;  it  is  in  the  Gothic 
Style,  with  large  and  lofty  Windows 
of  painted  Giass,  and  has  a  high 
Spire  with  8  Bells,  and  a  handsome 
Organ,  the  Gift  of  William  Henry, 
Earl  of  Powis  ;  and  a  Number  of  an- 
tique Monuments  and  Inscription?, 
particularly  one  relating  to  Prince 
Arthur,  Brother  to  Henry  VIII. 
whose  Bowels  were  deposited  here. 
Its  ancient  Castle,  standing  at  the 
west  End  of  the  Town,  is  supposed 
to  have  been  built  by  Roger  de 
Montgomery,  Earl  of  Shrewsbury, 
in  the  Reign  of  Henry  I.  ;  but  he 
rebelling  against  his  Sovereign,    it 


was  forfeited  to  the  Crown.  Various 
Possessors  appear  to  have  held  and 
been  deprived  of  Ludlow  Castle,  till 
the  Reign  of  Henry  VI.  when  Rich. 
Plantagenet,  Duke  of  York,  here  set 
up  his  Standard  ;  but  being  killed  at 
th,e  Battle  of  Wakefield,  it  was  seized 
by  the  King's  Forces,  and  disman- 
tled. Soon  after  this  his  Son  Edward 
got  Possession  of  it,  and  restored  the 
Fortress.  Milton's  Masque  of  Comus 
was  first  performed  here  during  the 
Earl  of  Bridgewater's Presidency, prin- 
cipally by  His  Lordship's  Sons  and 
Daughters  :  but  all  the  once  royal 
Apartments  and  Rooms  of  State  now 
lie  open,  the  whole  being  completely 
ruinous,  and  covered  with  Ivy.  Its 
Situation  is  beautiful,  and  the  Battle- 
ments are  of  great  Height  and  Thick- 
ness, with  Towers  at  convenient 
Distances. 

At  the  Vinalsj  near  Ludlow,  is  seen  a 
most  beautiful  Prospect. 

About  5  m.  on  1.  of  Ludlow  is  Downton 
Castle,  the  noble  Mansion  and  fine 
Walks  of  Rich.  Payne  Knight,  Esq. 

z  m.  from  Ludlow,  to  the  1.  on  the 
Banks  of  the  Teme  River,  is  Oakly 
Park,  Dowager  Lady  Clive. 

Onibury,  on  the  1.  is  Stone  House,  the

is  Fern  Hall,  Hurt  Sitwell,  Esq. 

Newton  Green,  \  m.  on  the  1.  is  Sibdon

Montgomery,  near,  on  the  r.  is  Lymoie

Montgomery  is  situated  within  two 
Miles  of  the  Severn,  and  was  for- 
merly surrounded  with  Walls.  The 
Castle  stands  on  an  Eminence  north 
of  the  Town,  and  appears  to  have 
been  a  very  stately  Building ;  little 
of  it  now  remains.  On  a  Hill  near 
the  Castle  is  a  stupendous  British 
Post ;  the  Approach  is  guarded  by  four 
great  Ditches,  having  two  or  three 
Entrances  toward  the  principal  Work.

Buckingham  is  a  very  ancient  Town,

the  Altar-piece,  representing  the

from  the  celebrated  Picture  of  Ra-- 
phael;  it  was  presented  to  the  Parish!

mon with  almost  the  whole  County.)

tues  ;  the  Gardens  arc  considered  the

Between  Tardebig  and  Bromesgro-ve  is

Bromesgrove  formerly  was  a  Borough 
Town:  it  is  governed  by  a  Bailiff, 
Recorder,  and  Aldermen.  It  has  a 
good  Grammar  School  founded  by 
K.  Edward  VI.  The  Church  stands 
on  a  Hill,  and  its  Tower  and  Spire 
are  said  to  be  the  neatest  in  the

Kidderminster,  within  i  m.  is  Commer- 
ton,  Jas.  Hooman,  Esq.;  near  which 
is  Park  Hall,  Jacob  Turner,  Esq. 

Kidderminster  is  governed  by  a  Recorder 
and  2  Magistrates,  called  the  Bailiff 
and  Justices  :  the  Bailiff,  who  is  one 
of  the  Quorum,  is  annually  elected 


by  his  brother  Aldermen,  12  in 
Number,  with  the  Concurrence  of 
the  25  Common  Councilmen.  It 
has  a  good  Grammar  School,  free 
for  all  the  Inhabitants  of  the  Town. 
The  Church  is  a  venerable  Gothic 
Structure,  and  the  Town  Hall  is 
large  and  commodious.  The  Scotch 
and  flat  Carpet,  known  by  the  Name 
of  Kidderminster,  is  the  principal 
Manufacture,  and  was  introduced 
here  about  1735. 

Alam  Bridge,  beyond,  on  r.  is  Coton 
Hall,  Col.  Gatacre. 

Quat,  1  m.  beyond,  on  1.  is  Dudmaston

Bridgenorth,  near,  on  1.  is  St.  James's, 
John  Stanier,  Esq. 

On  r.  of  Bridgenorth  are  Stanley  Hall, 
Sir  Frederick  Jones,  Bart ;  and  Gat' 
acre  Park,  Thomas  Gatacre,  Esq. 

Bridgenorth  is  a  Place  of  great  Trade  in 
the  Manufacture  of  Cloth,  Stockings, 
Iron  Tools,  &c.  The  Hill  on  which 
the  upper  Part  of  the  Town  stands 
rises  60  Yards  above  the  Bed  of  the 
River;  many  of  the  Houses  are 
founded  upon  the  Rock,  and  most 
of  the  Cellars  are  Caves  hewn  out  of 
it:  on  the  Proofs  of  the  Caves  are 
Gardens  with  Footpaths  over  them, 
so  that  Persons  may  walk  over  the 
Tops  of  several  of  the  Houses  with 
out  Danger ;  and  there  is  a  curious 
Walk  made  from  the  high  Part  of 
the  Town  to  the  Bridge,  being  a 
hollow  Way  hewn  20  Feet  through 
the  Depth  of  the  Rock.  The  Town 
is  governed  by  2  Bailiffs,  24  Alder 
men,  48  Common  Councilmen,  a 
Recorder,  Town  Clerk,  &c. 

Morley,  on  1.  Morvill  Hall,  late  Charles

is  Aldenham  Hall,  Sir  Ferdinand 
Richard  Acton,  Bart. 

WilUy,  on  1.  Cecil  Forester,  Esq.

Caughley  Place,  T.  Turner,   Esq. 

At  Broseley,  late  John  Wilkinson,  Esq. 
and  —  Forester,  Esq. 

t  m.  on  r.  of  Broseley,  Alex.  Brodie,  Esq. 

In  Broseley  and  its  Neighbourhood  are 
Iron  Works,  supposed  to  be  the  most 
considerable  in  the  Kingdom.

The  Trent  and  Mersey,   or  Grand  Trunk 


[302. 


Canal,  commences  from  the  Trent] 
River  at  Wildenferry,  passes  through; 
Swarkestone  (where  it  is  joined  by] 
the  Derby  Canal),  thence  to  near 
Burton  on  Trent  (to  which  Town  it 
has  a  Branch),  over  Fradley  Heath' 
(where  the  Fradley  Canal  connects 
with  it),  close  to  Rudgley,  and  thence 
to  Haywood  (where  the  Worce:ter- 
shire  and  Staffordshire  joins  it),  and 
proceeds  to  Stoke  (here  the  Caldon 
Branch  commences,  which  goes  to  a 
Place  of  that  Name,  a  Part  of  which 
is  by  Railway,  and  another  Branch 
which  goes  to  Newcastle  underLyne  . 
From  Stoke  the  Canal  proceeds  to 
Harecastle,  where  is  the  Harccastle 
Tunnel*,  2888  Yards  underground  ; 
thence  to  Middlewich,  and  near  to 
Northwich  and  Anderton,  to  Barnton 
Tunnel,  57Z  Yards  underground:  at 
a  little  Distance  is  the  Saliersfofd 
Tunnel.  From  thence  the  Canal  goes 
to  Dutton,  near  to  which  is  Preston 
Tunnel,  of  1241  Yards  underground, 
and  at  about  1  m.  it  connects  with 
the  Duke  of  Bridgewater's  Canal  at 
Preston  on  the  Hill,  which  unites  it 
with  the  Mersey  at  Runcorn,  and 
forms  an  uninterrupted  Navigation 
between  the  Ports  of  Hull  and  Liver-! 
pool.  Length  of  the  Trent  and  Mer-j 
sey  Canal,  93  m.;  of  the  Duke  of- 
Bridgewater's,  from  Preston  to  Run-* 
corn,  6  m.:    whole  Length  99  m.

The  Duks  of  Bridgeivater's  Canal  begins 
in  the  Township  of  Sa'ford  adjoining 
Manchester,  and  unites  with  the 
River  Mersey  at  Runcorn  Gap.  Its 
Course  from  Manchester  is  by  Stret- 
ford,  Altrincham,  Goppenhall, 
Daresbury,  and  Preston  on  the  Hill: 
here  it  is  joined  by  the  Trent  and 
Mersey  Canal,  and  proceeds  to 
Lower  Runcorn,  wheie  it  falls  84 
Feet  to  the  Mersey  by  10  Locks.  I 
Its  Line  to  Worseley  Mill  and  Leigh 
departs  from  the  main  Line  above 
described,  near  to  Stretford,  about 
3  m.  from  Manchester;  from  thence 
it  goes  to  the  Irwell,  and  by  a  nobie 


Aqueduct  is  carried  over  that  River, 
and  passes  to  Worseley  Mill,  which 
completes  His  Grace's  original  Plan; 
the  Extension  from  Worseley  to 
Leigh  being  of  late  Date,  and  on 
which  no  additional  Tonnage  is 
charged.  Whole  Length  of  the  Na- 
vigation, including  the  Extension  to 
Leigh,  36  m.  all  upon  a  Level  ;  in 
addition  to  which  there  are  about 
16  m.  of  Canal  underground,  within 
the  Mountain  at  Worseley. 

On  the  r.  of  Warrington  is  Bank  Hall, 
Thomas  Patten,  Esq. 

The  Sankey  Navigation  is  from  the  River 
Mersey,  a  little  South  of  Sankey 
Bridges,  where  it  locks  into  that 
River  ;  in  its  Course  from  thence  it 
passes  near  Little  Sankey,  and  by 
the  Side  of  the  Sankey  River,  which 
is  used  as  a  Feeder  to  the  Canal,  and 
terminates  at  St.  Hellen.  This  Canal 
was  the  first  executed  in  theKingdom. 

At  Bold  is  Bold  Hall,  Mrs.  Bold. 

Rainhill,  about  if  m.  on  1.  is  Red  Hall,

The  Derby  Canal  is  united  with  the  R. 
Derwent  at  Derby,  by  three  distinct 
Lines  :  the  southern  goes  by  Osmas- 
ton to  Swarkston,  where  it  crosses 
the  Trent  and  Mersey  Canal,  and 
then  unites  with  the  R.  Trent :  the 
eastern  Branch  runs  contiguous  to 
the  Derwent,  passes  by  Breaston,and 
joins  the  Erwash  Canal,  a  little  south 
of  Sandiacre:  the  northern  Branch 
running  at  a  small  Distance  from  the 
Derwent,  completes  its  Line  at  Little 
Eaton  :  whole  Length  17  m. 

!Near  Derby,  on  r.  is  Castle  Field,  — 

j     Burrows,  Esq.

royal  Borough  in  the  Reign  of  Ed- 
ward the  Confessor.  It  is  governed 
by  a  Mayor,  High  Steward,  9  Alder- 
men, a  Recorder,   14  Brothers,    14

Burgesses,  Town  Clerk,  ike.  In  this 
Town  are  some  extensive  Silk  Mills, 
upon  a  most  ingenious  Plan,  the 
first  of  which  was  erected  from  a 
Model  brought  from  Italy.  In  this 
Machine  are  nearly  100,000  Move- 
ments put  into  Action  by  a  single 
Wheel,  any  one  of  which  may  be 
stopped  at  Pleasure.  Every  Time 
this  Wheel  goes  round,  which  is 
three  Times  in  a  Minute,  the  Ma 
chine  works  73,728  Yards  of  Silk 
Derby  has  also  a  very  extensive  Ma 
nufactory  of  Porcelain  ;  and  a  Num- 
ber of  Persons  are  here  employed  in 
turning  Vases,  Urns,  and  various 
Chimney  Ornaments,  &c  of  Marble, 
Spar,  and  Petrifications,  which 
abound  in  this  Vicinity.  The

ing, enriched  with  a  beautiful  Gothic

The   Manchester  and  Ashton  under  Lyne\ 
Canal  commences  at  Manchester  and 
goes  to  Clayton,  and  thence  to  Fair- 
field, where    it     divides     into     two 
Branches,  one  to  Ashton  under  Lyne 
(where  it  connects  with  the  Hudders- 
field  and  Peak  Forest  Canals),  and 
the  other  to  the  Aqueduct  nearWater 
houses  :  it  here  divides  again  into  two 
more  Branches  ;  one   goes  to   Fair 
bottom,  the  other  to  Hollinwood,  the 
latter  called  the  Wemeth  Branch, 
At  Clayton,  as  above,  there  is  also  a 
Branch  which  goes  to  Heaton  Norris 
near  Stockport.     The  Length  of  this 
Canal,  including  its  several  Branches 
is   upwards   of   17    M.  upon  which 
there  are  25  Locks. 

Manchester    is    not    an     incorporated 
Town,  and   is   governed  only  as   a 
Manor,  by  Courts  Leet  and  Baron 
It  has  a  collegiate  Church,  which  is 
a  handsome  Gothic  Structure,  orna- 
mented with  some  beautiful   Sculp 
ture.       The    Tabernacle    Work    is 
very   curious,    and    it   has   a   large 
and   powerful   Organ.      The   colle 
giate  Body  consists  of  a  Warden,  4 
Fellows,  2  Chaplains,  2  Clerks, 
Choristers,  and  4  Singing-men.-     Be- 
sides the  collegiate  Church  it  has  ten 
others;  also  an  Hospital,  free  School 
and  Library,  each  of  them  well   en 
do  wed.     The  Theatre  is  a  very  neat 
Building:  the  Gentleman's  Concert 
Room  is  elegant  and  capacious,  and 
will   accommodate     1200    Persons: 
there  are  also  new  and  commodious 
Assembly  Rooms.     Manufactures  of 
the  greatest  Extent  are  carried  on  in 
Manchester  and   its   Neighbourhood 
but  the  most  important  Branch  is  in 
the  Cotton  Trade.     It  is  also  noted 
for  its  Velverets  and  Checks,  Tapes 
Laces,  Gartering,  &c.     The  Town  i 
well  paved  and  lighted, and  is  supplied 
with  Water,  after  the  Manner  of  Lon- 
don, by  means  of  underground  Pipes. 

The  Bolton  and  Bury  Canal  commences 
at  Manchester,  runs  some  Way  close 
to  the  River  Irwell,  crosses  it  near 
Clifton,  and  then  passes  by  its  Side 
to  Bolton,  crossing  the  River  Roch 
in  its  Way,  from  whence  a  Branch? 
goes  to  Bury.

Lancaster  is  seated  on  the  R.  Loyne, 
which  forms  a  Harbour  of  mode- 
rate Size  :  the  Merchant  Shipping  is 
chiefly  employed  in  the  West  India, 
American,  and  Baltic  Trades  :  it  has 
a  long  fine  Quay,  on  which  is  a  Suite 
of  noble  Warehouses.  The  Church  is 
a  handsome  Gothic  Structure.  The 
Town  Hall  and  Exchange  is  a  good 
Building,  and  has  a  noble  Portico. 
The  Castle  is  said  by  some  to  have 
been  built  in  the  Time  of  Adrian  ; 
but  the  present  Structure  was  erected 
in  the  Time  of  Edward  III.  On  the 
Top  is  a  large  square  Tower,  called 
John  of  Gaunt's  Chair,  whence  is  a 
most  extensive  Prospect.  In  this 
Castle  the  Assizes  are  held,  and  it  is 
the  County  Gaol. 

5  m.  N.  E.  of  Lancaster  is  a  remarkable 
Cavern,  called  Dunald  Mill  Hole;< 
a  large  Brook  runs  in  at  its  Mouth 
by  several  beautiful  Cascades,  whence 
continuing  its  Course  for  two  Miles 
under  a  large  Mountain,  it  makes 
its  Appearance  again  at  Carnforth. 

About  1  M.  from  Lancaster,  on  r.  is 
BeamontHall,  E.  F.  Buckley,  Esq.; 
beyond  which  is  Hal  ton  Hp.11,  W.  B. 
Bradshaw,  Esq. 

Between  Bolton  and  Cart/forth  is  a  fine 
View  over  the  Lancaster  Sands. 

About  2  m.  beyond  Carnforth,  on  r,  are 
the  Ruins  of  Borwick  Hall. 

Burton,  entering,  on  r.  Capt.  Stovin. 

Kendal,  situated  on  the  River  Ken,  js 
a  Place  of  considerable  Trade;  its 
chief  Manufactures  areCottons.coarse 
Woollens,  Linseys,  Druggets,  Wor- 
sted Stockings,  Flannels,  Jmd  Serges. 
It  has  seven  trading  Companies,  each 
having  its  Hall ;  viz.  Mercers,  Tan- 
ners,Glovers, Shearmen,Cordwainers, 
Tailors,  and  Pewterers.  The  Church 
is  a  Gothic  Structure  ;  and  there  are 
the  Remains  of  an  ancient  Castle. 

On  r.  of  Kendal  is  Abbot  Hall,  —

■Penrith  was  originally  claimed  by  and 
belonged  to  the  Scots ;  but  being 
disputed  by  the  English,  it  was  twice 
burnt  in  the  Reigns  of  Edward  III. 
and  Rich.  II.  Its  Church  is  a  large 
handsome  Structure,  and  it  has  a 
good  Free  School  and  Charity  School. 
On  the  North  Bank  of  the  R.  Emont' 
are  two  Caves  or  Grottos,  dugout  of; 
the  solid  Rock,  and  very  extensive  : 
the  Passage  to  them  is  narrow  and 
dangerous, and  it  is  supposed  they  were 
intended  as  a  Place  of  Safety  during 
theIncursionsoftheScots.(Seep.358.)

j  Carlisle  is  a  Bishop's  See,  and  was  for 

1  merly  Part  of  the  Diocese  of  Dur- 
ham, but  made  a  distinct  Bishopric 
by  Henry  I.  Being  a  Frontier  Town, 
it  is  fortified  with  a  Wall,  a  Citadel, 
and  a  Castle.  The  Wall  was  first 
built  by  Egfrid,  King  of  Northum- 
berland, in  the  7th  Century ;  and 
the  Citadel  and  Castle  by  William 
Rufus.  The  Wall  has  three  Gates 
or  Entrances  into  the  City:  the  Eng- 
lish Gate  to  the  South  ;  the  Scotch 
Gate  to  the  North  ;  and  the  Irish 
Gate  to  the  West.  The  Picts  Wall, 
which  was  built  across  the  Country 
from  Newcastle,  terminates  near  this 


Place.  It  was  once  strongly  fortified, 
but  its  Castle  and  Walls  are  now  in  a 
State  of  Decay.  It  was  taken  by  the 
Rebels  in  1745,  but  retaken  three 
Weeks  afterwards  by  the  Duke  of 
Cumberland:  in  it  the  unfortunate 
Mary  Queen  of  Scots  was  confined 
Principal  Manufactures, Cotton  Yarn, 
Cotton  and  Linen  Checks,  printed 
Cottons,  Osnaburghs,  Drills,  Worsted 
Shags,  tanned  Leather,  &c.  &c.

Neivarb :  this  Town  was  incorporated 
by  Charies  II.  in  Gratitude  for  its 
Loyalty  to  his  Father,  who  granted 
it  the  Privilege  of  sending  Members 
to  Parliament.  It  is  governed  by  a 
Mayor  and  12  Aldermen.  The  Town 
Hall  is  a  magnificent  Stone  Building. 
The  Church,  esteemed  one  of  the 
finest  in  the  Kingdom,  was  erected 
by  Henry  IV.  Of  its  ancient  Castle, 
built  in  the  Reign  of  King  Stephen, 
there  now  remain  only  some  of  the 
Walls,  of  great  Thickness  and  Height. 
The  Town  is  neat,  and  many  of  the 
Buildings  are  new  ;  and  the  Market- 
place, though  not  spacious,  is  ex- 
tremely handsome.  In  consequence 
of  the  many  Inundations  from  the 
River,  which  often  rendered  the 
Town  impassable,  a  new  Turnpike 
Road  was  made  about  the  Year  1 770, 
and  raised  so  high  upon  Arches,  as 
to  be  passed  with  Safety  in  the  great- 
est Floods  :  it  was  constructed  under 
the  Direction  of  Mr.  Smeaton  ;  and 
near  the  Town  there  is  a  Bridge,  for 
the  same  Purpose,  made  mostly  upon 
dry  Land.

Doncaster  is  seated  on  the  River  Don 
over  which  it  has  two  Bridges,  and 
whence  it  takes  its  Name.  Th 
Parish  Church  is  a  very  ancient 
Structure;  its  Steeple  is  a  Piece  of 
excellent  Workmanship :  in  the 
Church  is  an  Epitaph  dated  1597, 
to  the  Memory  of  one  Robert  Byrks, 
who  gave  Rossington  Wood  to  the 
Poor  of  the  Parish.  Its  Castle,  to- 
gether with  the  whole  Town,  was 
destroyed  by  Fire  in  759  ;  the  former 
was  never  afterwards  rebuilt.  In  the 
Reign  of  Henry  III.  a  Convent  was 
founded  here,  and  an  Hospital  for 
Lepers.  The  Situation  of  the  Town 
is  remarkably  pleasant.  The  Man- 
sion House  of  Doncaster  is  a  very 
spacious  Stone  Building.  It  has  a 
handsome  Theatre  and  Town  Hall  j 
also  a  free  Grammar  School,  Alms 
House,  and  a  public  Dispensary.  At 
the  north  End  of  Freres  Bridge  was 
a  House  of  White  Friars,  and  near 
it,  another  of  Grey  Friars  The  Re- 
mains of  a  Roman  Highway  are  still 
visible  here.  The  Town  is  governed 
by  a  Mayor,  Recorder,  and  Common 
Council,  and  formerly  sent  Members 
to  Parliament.  Its  chief  Manufac- 
ture is  that  of  spinning  Wool  and 
Cotton.

built:  m  the  Centre  of  the  Town  is 
a  Cross  or  Obelisk,  12  Feet  high. 
Many  Roman  Coins  have  been  found 
in  this  Place,  and  in  a  Field  near  the 
Bridge  are  four  large  Stones, called  the 
Dev  il's  Arrows,  supposed  to  have  been 
placed  there  by  the  Romans  to  mark 
the  Roads.  It  is  a  Corporation,  and 
sends  2  Members  to  Parliament.  In 
this  Neighbourhood  was  fought  a 
bloody  Battle  in  the  Reign  of  Edward 
III.  in  1332,  in  which  the  Earl  of 
•Lancaster  was  taken  Prisoner,  and 
afterwards  executed  with  several 
other  Nobles. 

Lee  wing,  if  m.  beyond,  on  r.  Leases 
Hall,  Mrs.  Ardens  ;  and  about  4  m. 
from  Leeming,  on  1.  Hornby  Castle, 
Duke  of  Leeds. 

Catterick  is  a  Place  of  great  Antiquity, 
and  was  burned  in  769  by  Eanred, 
King  of  Northumberland:  its  an- 
cient Name,  Catturacton,  seems  to 
have  been  derived  from  a  Cataract  or 
Waterfall ;  near  it  is  the  River  Swale, 
over  which  it  has  a  Bridge,  where 
also  one  of  the  Roman  Roads  crosses 
the  River :  on  its  Banks  are  still  the 
Foundations  of  an  ancient  Castle, 
and  many  Roman  Coins  and  Urns 
have  been  dug  up  here. 

On  the  1.  of  Catterick  is  Brough  Hall, 
late  Sir  John  Lavvson,  Bart. 

The  Three  Tuns,  on  the  1.  of,  are  Ask 
Hall,  Lord  Dundas ;  and  Gilling 
Hall,  Lady  Wharton  ;  and  about  1 
M.  beyond  The  Three  Tuns,  on  \)  is

Hildyard,  Bart.

ritt,  Esq. 

Brough  is  situated  about  2  m.  from  the 
River  Eden  •,  it  has  a  neat  Church  a 
little  Way  from  the  Town,  the  Pulpit 
of  which  is  cut  out' of  one  entire 
Stone  :  near  the  Church,  oh  a  Hill, 
are  the  Ruins  of  an  ancient  .Castle, I 
belonging  to  the  Earl  of  Thanet ; 
Part  of  the  Tower  was  standing  till 
1792,  when  it  mostly  fell  down  ;  on, 
digging  near  the  Ruins  an  Urn  full 
of  Roman  Coins  was  found,  from 
which  it  appears  to  have  been  built 
in  the  Time  of  the  Romans.   On  the 


Left  of  the  Castle  the  Prospect  is 
closed  by  a  Range  of  craggy  Moun- 
tains, over  the  Tops  of 'which  Shrubs 
and  Trees  are  promiscuotisly  scat- 
tered :  to  the  r.  is  an  extensive  fertile 
Plain  ;  and  behind,  the  lofty  Pro- 
montory of  Wiidmore  Fell  lifts  its 
Brow,  and  terminates  the  Prospect. 

Appleby  is  almost  surrounded  by  the 
River  Eden:  it  was  a  Roman  Station 
called  Aballaba,  and  had  a  military 
Way  crossing  the  Country  here 
The  Assizes  are  held  in  the  Town 
Hall,  and  the  Judges  lodge  in  the 
Castle,  an  ancient  Building  at  the 
End  of  the  principal  Street,  belong- 
ing to  the  Earl  of  Thanet.  It  is 
Borough  Town,  and  sends  z  Mem- 
bers to  Parliament ;  and  is  governed 
by  a  Mayor,  Aldermen,  and  Com- 
mon Council:  besides  its  Church, 
an  old  Building  which  stands  at  the 
End  of  the  Town,  there  is  another 
in  Bongate.  It  has  a  Gaol,'  Town 
Hall,  Charity  School,  Free  School 
(endowed  with  a  Salary  of  1 20/.  a 
Year),  and  an  Hospital '  for. a  Go- 
verness arid  twelve"  Widows,1  com- 
monly called  the  Mother  and  twelve 
Sisters.  This  Town  was  taken  by 
Surprise  by  William  King  of  Scot- 
land,  but  recovered  by  King  John  ; 
and  Henry  II.  granted  it  .Privileges 
equal  to  trie  City  of  York :  in  the 
Reigns  of  Henry  II.  and  Richard  II. 
it  was  set  on  Fire  by  the  Scots  ;  and 
•  in  1598  it  suffered  greatly  by  Pesti- 
lence, since  which  Time  it  has  never 
recovered  its  original  Extent.

Oakham  is  remarkable  for  an  ancient 
Custom  observed  there,  that  the  first 
Time  any  Peer  of  the  Realm  comes 
within  the  Precinct  of  this  Lordship, 
he  forfeits  a  Shoe  from  the  Horse  he 
rides  on  to  the  Lord  of  the  Castle  or 
Manor,  unless  he  chooses  to  com- 
mute for  it :  several  Horse  Shoes, 
gilt,  and  of  curious  Workmanship, 
are  in  consequence  nailed  on  the 
Castle  Hall  Door,  some  of  them 
being  stamped  with  the  Names  of 
the  Donors.  Of  its  ancient  Castle 
there  now  remains  only  a  Part  of 
the  Walls.

The  Chesterfield  Canal  commences  at 
the  Town  of  Chesterfield,  passes  by 
the  River  Rother  as  far  asKillamarsh, 
and  enters  Yorkshire :  at  Harthill 
in  that  County  it  is  carried  by  a 
Tunnel  30CO  Yards  underground  ; 
then  passes  into  Nottinghamshire, 
goes  a  little  north  of  Worksop,  crosses 
the  Idle  R.  at  East  Retford,  and 
thence  to  Misterton,  where  it  joins 
the  R.  Trent.  Length  46  m.

Barnsley  is  seated  on  the  Side  of  a  Hill,

nufacture of  Wire,  Nails,  Hardware,

Bottles.

Huddersfield  is  a  large  and  populous 
Town,  and  carries  on  a  most  exten- 
sive Trade  in  the  Manufacture  of 
Serges,  Kerseymeres,  Freize,  and 
narrow  and  broad  Cloths.  It  has  a 
spacious  Cloth  Hall :  the  Cloth  Mar- 
ket is  held  on  Tuesday.  Two  Miles 
south  of  the  Town,  on  Castle  Hill, 
are  still  visible  the  Remains  of  the 
ancient  City  of  Canbodunum.    - 

Clough  Cliff,  1  m.  on  r.  is  Fixby  Hall,,

Halifax  is  a  very  ancient,  populous,  and 
flourishing  Town.  The  Woollen  Ma- 
nufacture has  long  been  established, 
here,  and  of  late  Years  there  have 
been  erected  numerous  Mills  and 
Machinery  for  the  Cotton  Manufac- 
tory. The  principal  Articles  manu- 
factured in  and  about  Halifax  are 
Shalloons,  Lastings,  and  Amens, 
Russets  or  Florentines,  Supebarragans 
or  Serge  Imperial,  Serge  Moreens, 
Tammies,  Calimancoes,  &c.  There 
has  been  erected  an  elegant  Edifice, 
called  the  Piece  Hall,  occupying  a 
Space  of  io,oeo  square  Yards,  hav- 
ing 315  distinct  Rooms  for  the  Lodg- 
ment of  Goods,  which  are  open  for 
Sale  once  a  Week.  The  Church  is 
an  old  and  venerable  Building,  and 
contains  a  Number  of  Monuments  ; 
it  has  1  1  Chapels  of  Ease.

I  the  Town  of  Leeds  to  Liverpool, 
forming  a  Line  of  Canal,  when  com- 
pleted, of  129  m.  Its  first  Act  was 
obtained  in  the  Year  1770,  and  after 

j  executing  a  very  considerable  Por-j 
tion,  en  the  Yorkshire  and  on  the! 
Lancashire   Sides,  an  Act  was   ob-i 


405] 


Roads  measured  from  Hicks's  Hall. 


[406 


tained,  in  1790,  for  varying  the  Re- 
mainder of  the  Line;  and  a  third 
Act  was  passed  in  1794,  again  to 
vary  the  Line  from  near  Colne  to 
Wigan  :  this  Part  of  the  Canal! 
is  called  the  Deviation  Line,  the 
whole  of  which  is  not  yet  completed. 
The  Part  from  Liverpool  to  Nevvbo- 
rough  is  calied  the  Lancashire  Side  ; 
and  from  Newborough  to  Wigan  (a 
Distance  of  7  m.),  the  Upper  Douglasj 
Navigation.  From  Leeds  to  near 
Colne  is  called  the  Yorkshire  Side  of' 
the  Leeds  and  Liverp.  >ol  Canal,  which; 
commences  at  Leeds,  and  passes  on! 
the  south  Side  of  the  River  Aire,  by j 
Calverley  and  Idle  to  Shipley  (where 
it  is  joined  by  the  Bradford  Canal,! 
which  comes  from  the  Town  of 
Bradford,  and  is  about  3  m.  in' 
Length),  and  at  about  1  m.  it  crosses 
the  Aire  and  goes  by  its  Side  as  far  as 
Gargrave,  passing  by  Bingley,  near 
to  Keighley,  through  Kildwick  and 
Skipton  to  Gargrave,  and  thence  by 
Church  Marton  and  Thornton,  to  its 
Summit  at  the  Village  of  FoulridgeJ 
where  it  passes  underground  1630! 
Yards,  by  a  Tunnel,  which  is  18 
Feet  high  and  17  Feet  wide:  from 
hence  it  goes  to  Great  Marsden,  near 
Colne,  which  completes  that  Part  of 
the  Leeds  and  Liverpool  Canal  called 
the  Yorkshire  Side.  Here  com- 
mences the  Deviation  Line,  and  its 
Course  is  by  the  Market  Towns  of 
Burnley,  Blackburn,  and  Chorley, 
to  Wigan,  and  thence  to  Newbo- 
rough :  at  this  Place  commences  the 
Division  of  the  Canal  called  the 
Lancashire  Side,  which  proceeds  to 
Brier's  Mill  (where  a  Cut  is  made 
from  it,  called  the  Lower  Douglas 
Navigation,  of  about  5  m.  in  Length), 
and  from  thence  it  goes  to  Halsall, 
about  3  m.  N.  of  Ormskirk,  and  by 
Maghall,  &c.  to  Liverpool.  Lengths 
— Yorkshire  Side,  45  m.;  Deviation 
Line,  49  ;  Upper  Douglas,  7  ;  Lan- 
cashire Side,  28.

On  the  1.  ©f  Huntingdon  are  Hinchin- 
brook  House,  Earl  of  Sandwich;  and 
The  Views,  George  Sharpe,  Esq. 

Huntingdon  is  situated  near  the  River 
Ouse,  over  which  it  has  a  good  Free- 
stone Bridge,  of  six  Arches.  From 
its  ancient  convenient  Neighbour- 
hood for  Hunting,  it  is  supposed  to 

have   derived    its   Name Hunton 

Down  ;  and  was  originally  built  on 
a  Spot  that  was  an  entire  Forest. 
Near  the  Church  of  St.  Mary  was 
anciently  a  Priory  of  Black  Canons. 
On  an  Eminence  near  the  Town 
stood  a  Castle,  erected  by  Edward 
the  Elder,  and  enlarged  by  David 
the  First  of  Scotland,  Earl  of  Hunt- 
ingdon. The  Town  is  recorded  to 
have  formerly  had  fifteen  Parish 
Churches,  but  now  there  are  only 
two,  in  one  of  which  is  an  ancient 
Steeple.  It  now  chiefly  consists  of 
one  principal  Street,  and  is  well 
paved,  and  lighted  during  the  Win- 
ter. The  Town  Hall,  in  which  the 
Assizes  are  held,  is  a  commodious 
and  neat  Building,  standing  on  one 
Side  of  a  large  Square.  Here  is  also 
a  good  Free  and  Grammar  School. 
The  Ouse  being  navigable  to  Bedford, 
it  derives  a  great  Advantage  in  its 
Supply  of  Coals,  &c.  from  Lynn  by 
Barges.  Huntingdon  is  governed  by 
a  Mayor,  12  Aldermen,  and  a  Com- 
mon Council,  and  sends  2  Members 
to  Parliament.

North  Allerton  consists  principally  of 
one  Street,  of  about  ■§  a  Mile  long. 
The  Church  is  a  Gothic  Structure 
built  in  the  Form  of  a  Cross,  and 
contains  several  handsome  Monu 
ments.  Among  the  other  Improve 
ments  of  the  Town  is  a  new  Prison, 
erected  on  Mr.  Howard's  Plan  ;  it 
consists  of  30  Cells,  with  4  strong 
ones  for  capital  Offenders  ;  and  a 
Place  for  Correction  and  Labour 
Here  formerly  was  an  ancient  Castle, 
which  was  much  enlarged  by  Bishop 
Pudsey ;  but  was  seized  and  destroy 
ed  by  Henry  II.  A  small  Convent 
for  Monks,  of  the  Cistertian  Order, 
was  founded  here  by  Edward  I.  but 
no  Remains  are  extant.  The  whole 
of  the  Manor  has  been  subject  to 
the  Bishop  of  Durham  from  the  Time 
of  William  Rufus.  He  appoints  a 
Bailiff  for  Life,  who  presides  at  the 
Election  for  Members  of  Parliament, 
who  are  chosen  by  the  whole  of  the 
Housekeepers  that  pay  Scot  and  Lot. 
Near  this  Place  was  fought  the  cele- 
brated Battle  between  the  English  and 
Scots,  called  the  Battle  of  the  Stan- 
dard, in  1138:  the  Spot  where  it  was 
fought  retains  the  Name  of  Standard 
Hill  ;  and  some  Caverns  near  it  are 
supposed  to  have  been  the  Places 
wher$  the  Scots  were  buried. 

About  1  M.  from  Lcvesome  Hill,  on  1. 
is  Hutton  Bonville  Hall,  Anthony 
Hammond,   Esq.

Durham:  this  City  is  supposed  to  have 
been  first  built  in  995  ;  it  is  nearly 
surrounded  by  the  River  Wear,  and 
is  about  a  Mile  square.  The  Cathe- 
dral and  Castle  stand  upon  an  Emi- 
nece,  inclosed  by  the  Remains  of 
the  old  City  Walls.  The  Situation 
of  the  Cathedral  is  extremely  grand, 
the  Building  stretching  along  the 
Crown  of  an  Eminence  80  Feet  per- 
pendicular from  the  Surface  of  the 
River  which  washes  its  Base  :  before 
it  is  a  large  open  Area,  called  the 
Palace  Green,' on  the  north  Side  of 
which  stands  the  Castle,  first  erected 
by  William  the  Conqueror ;  it  for- 
merly contained  four  Tiers  of  Apart- 
ments, but  nothing  now  remains 
except  the  Mount  Vaults,  and  Part 
of  the  Shell.  In  a  deep  Vale  near 
the  River  are  the  Remains  of  Finch- 
all  Abbey,  founded  in  1196  for  Be- 
nedictine Monks.  At  Durham  is  the 
Palace  of  the  Bishop  of  the  Diocese. 
1  m.  beyond  Durham,  on  r.  is  Aycley 
Head,  Francis  Johnson,  Esq. ;  and 
\\  N.  E.  of  Durham  is  Newton  Hall, 
Rev.  Mr.  Fawcett. 

Plamtvorth,  about  2  m.  on  r.  is  Cocken 

Hall,  Carr  Ibbetson,  Esq.

m.  on  1.  of  which  is  Gibside,  Earl  of

Newcastle:  this  Place  has  long  been 
noted  for  its  Glass  Works,  particularly 
in  the  finer  Sort ;  and  in  the  Coal 
Trade  it  is  the  first  Port  in  the 
World,  and  has  sometimes  exported 
to  foreign  Parts  and  coastwise,  up- 
wards of  600,060  Chaldrons  in  a 
Year.  It  contains  4  Churches  ;  and 
that  of  St.  Nicholas,  the  Mother 
Church,  is  a  most  curious  Fabric 
erected  by  David  King  of  Scotland. 
The  Bridge  over  the  Tyne,  built 
about  1 775,  consists  of  9  large  elliptic 
Arches,  and  supports  a  Street  of 
Houses.  It  is  governed  by  a  Mayor 
Sheriff',  and  12  Aldermen,  and  has 
sent  Members  to  Parliament  ever 
since  the  Reign  of  Edward  I.

York :  this  is  the  only  City  in  England 
whose  chief  Magistrate  is  honoured 
with  the  Title  of  Lord,except  London. 
It  is  a  County  of  itself;  and  the  Go- 
vernment of  the  City  is  vested  in  the 
Lord  Mayor,  a  Recorder,  12  Alder- 
men, 2  Sheriffs,  8  Chamberlains,  24 
Common  Councilmen,  22  Assistants, 
a  Town  Clerk,  and  other  inferior 
Officers.  There  are  23  Parish 
Churches,  besides  the  Minster  or 
Cathedral :  this  stately  Structure  \i 
the  largest  Gothic  Church  in  Eng< 
land,  being  in  Length  524  Feet;  the 
Breadth  of  the  cross  Aisle,  222  J  the 
Height  of  the  Lantern,  180;  the 
Breadth  of  the  west  Front,  109  ;  and 
the  east,  105.  The  Castle,  originally 
built  by  Richard  III.  is  used  as  a 
Prison:  the  Castle  Walls  are  1103 
Yards  in  Circumference  :  adjoining 
the  Castle  is  a  high  Mound,  on  which 
stands  the  Shell  of  a  Tower  called 
Clifford's  Tower,  formerly  mounted 
with  Cannon  and  a  Garrison.  Yorfc 
sends  two  Members  to  Parliament

Lincoln  is  a  very  ancient  City,  and  was 
formerly  surrounded  with  Walls,  and 
defended  byTowers :  the  north  Roman 
Gate  of  1  he  City,called  Newport  Gate, 
still  remains,  and  is  one  of  the  noblest 
Remnants  of  Roman  Architecture  left 
in  Britain.  Lincoln  was  erected  into 
a  Bishopric  in  the  Year  1088  :  the  Ca- 
thedral is  a  magnificent  Fabric,  situ-

the  great  cast  Window-  was  fitted  up

York  in  j  762.  In  the  north  Tower,

Bell  called  Great  Tom  of  Lincoln  ;  it 
weighs  96  cwt.  3  qrs.  18  lb.  and  will 
hold  424  Gallons  Ale  Measure  :  the 
Circumference  is  22  Feet,  8  Inches: 
on  account  of  its  great  Weight  it 
has  not  been  rung  for  several  Years. 
Lincoln  is  governed  by  a  Mayor,  12

CROSS     ROADS 


The  Course  of  the  Rivers  and  navigable  Canals,  the  Population  and- Number 
of  Houses  in  the  Market  Towns,  with  the  Arrival  and  Departure  of  the 
Mail,  &c.  having  been  already  given  in  the  Direct  Roads,  it  is  judged  un 
necessary  to  repeat  them  here.  Those  Places  which  supply  Post  Horses  are 
noticed  at  the  End  of  each  Route,  and  the  Names  of  the  Inn*  will  be  seen 
by  referring  to  the  same  Places  on  the  Direct  Roads  from  London.

PACKET   BOATS; 

With  the  Dat/s  on  which  they  sail  from  their  respective  Ports, 


At  Pom  Patrick,  for  Donaghadee. 
Th  e  Packet  sails  at  One  P.  M.  daily ;  Wind  and  Weather  permitting. — Distance 
Seven  Leagues. 

At  Holyhead,  for  Dublin. 
Do.  Do.  Two  P.  AT.  daily. — Distance  23  Leagues. — Returns  every  Day  from 
Dublin,  Sundays  excepted. 

Sit  Milford,  for  Waterford. 
Do.  Do.  Do.  daily.  -  Distance  50  Leagues. 

At  Falmouth,  for  the  West  Indies. 
Mails  are  made  up  at  the  General  Post  Office  for  the  West  Indies  tv/iee  a 
Month  ;  on  the  Fust  Wednesday  tor  Jamaica  and  the  Leeward  Islands,  and  i  n 
the  Third  Wednesday  for  the  Leeward  Islands  only.  •  A  Mail  is  also  made  up 
the  Second  Wednesday  in  every  Month  for  Suiinam,  Demerara,  and  Berbice. 
The  Mail  arrives  at  Falmouth  late  on  Saturday  Evening;  and  the  Packet  sails 
en  Sunday  Morning,  if  it  has  sailing  Orders  from  the  Secretary  of  State. 

At  Falmouth,  for  America. 
Malls  are  made  up  in  London  the  First  Wednesday  of  every  Month  for 
Halifax,  Quebec,  and  New  York.  The  Packet  sails  from  Falmouth  soon  after 
the  Arrival  of  the  Mails  on  the  Saturday  Evening,  if  it  has  sailing  Orders  from 
the  Secretary  of  State  ;  and  goes  and  returns  by  the  Way  of  Halifax,  to  and 
ftom  New  York,  every  Month  ;  except  November,  December,  January,  and 
February,  during  which  Months  it  goes  and  returns  to  New  York  direct. 

At  Faxmouth,  for  Lisbon. 

The  Mail  for  Lisbon  is  made  up  every  Tuesday  Night,  and  sent  from  Fal- 
mouth generally  on  the  Saturday  Morning,  if  a  Packet  be  in  the  Harbour. 

At  Falmouth,  for  Madeira  and  the  Brazils. 
The  Mail  is  made  up   the  First  Tuesday  in  every  Month,  and  sails  on  the 
Saturday  following. 

At  Falmouth,  for  Gibraltar  and  the  Mediterranean. 
The  Mail  is  made  up  every  Third  Tuesday,  and  sails  on  the  Saturday  fol- 
lowing. 

At  Dover,  for  Calais. 
The  Mail  for  Calais  is  made  up  at  the  General  Po<t  Office  every  Tuesday, 
"Wednesday,    Thursday,    and   Friday  Night,    at   Twelve   o'Clock,    and  sails 
immediately  on  the  Arrival  of  the  Post. — Distance  Eight  Leagues. 
At  Harwich,  for  Holland,  &c. 
The  Mails  for  Holland,  Gottenburgh,  and  Hamburgh,  are  made  up  at  the 
General  Post  Office  every  Tuesday  and  Friday  Night,  at  Twelve  o'Clock,  and 
sails  immediately  on  the  Arrival  of  the  Post. 

At  Weymouth,  for  Guernsey  and  Jersey. 
The  Mail  is  made  up  every  Tuesday  and  Friday  Night  in  London.     Sails  on 
Wednesday  and  Saturday  from  Weymouth  about  Four  or  Five  o'Clock  in  the 
Afternoon;    Wind   and    Weather   permitting.      Returns    to  Weymouth   the 

Thursday  or  Friday  following. — Distance  35  Leagues. 

At  Whitehaven,  for  the  Isle  of  Man. 
The  Packet  Boat  carrying  the  Letters  to  and  from  the  Isle  of  Man,  sails  from 
Whitehaven  once  a  Week,  every  Tuesday,  and  returns  as  often. 
At  Ilfracomb,  for  Wales. 
The  Packet  sails  for  Swansea  every  Monday  and  Thursday,  and  returns  every* 
Tuesday  and  Saturday  ;  Wind  and  Weather  pel  mining.
